terroir.climate: Maritime Mediterranean with the smallest swing between seasons of any Australian region. Winters are mild and wet, with around 1,100 millimetres of rain falling almost entirely between May and September; summers are warm, dry and breezy rather than hot. The Leeuwin Current, a warm flow running south along the coast, keeps winter frost away and spring even, so budburst and flowering are seldom disturbed. Vintage variation is low, which is the region's commercial strength.
terroir.soils: Gravelly, ironstone-flecked sandy loams over granite and gneiss of the Leeuwin-Naturaliste Ridge, free draining and low in fertility: the famous Forest Grove gravels. Nearer the coast the ancient rock gives way to limestone and dune sand, the limestone that holds the region's caves. Vines on the gravel carry moderate vigour and ripen Cabernet with fine, dusty tannin.
terroir.topography: A low ridge running roughly 100 kilometres north to south between the two capes and up to about 27 kilometres wide, the land gently rolling rather than steep, most vineyards between sea level and 100 metres among jarrah and marri forest. The ridge divides a thin coastal strip from the slightly warmer, more sheltered inland side.
terroir.water: The Indian Ocean on the west and Geographe Bay to the north supply the breezes and the Leeuwin Current the warmth. The Margaret River itself is a small stream that gives the town and the region their name; it matters less to the vines than the sea does.

traps: Margaret River is maritime and even, not hot: its Cabernet is medium-bodied and cedary, nearer Bordeaux than Barossa.
The Leeuwin Current is a warm current, not a cold one; it moderates winter and spring rather than chilling the summer.
The six districts are unofficial; only Margaret River itself is a registered GI, within the South West Australia zone.
SSB and SBS are the same blend with the proportions reversed; the first grape named is the larger share.
The region's Chardonnay clone is Gingin, after a Western Australian town, not a French clone; some books call it the Mendoza clone.
The Margaret River itself is a small stream; the region's water is the ocean on three sides.

wines.note: Blackcurrant, cedar and bay leaf over fine gravelly tannin, medium to full in body at moderate alcohol, often with Merlot and Malbec in support. Decant a young one; it keeps for twenty years. Lamb with rosemary, beef with a red wine sauce.

Concentrated and long, white peach and grapefruit with a struck-match edge from barrel fermentation, acidity firm enough to age a decade. Serve cool rather than cold, with roasted chicken, crab or a cream sauce.
The region's everyday white, zesty, grassy and lime-fresh, usually unoaked and bottled under screwcap for drinking within two years. Oysters, ceviche and goat's cheese.
A softer Bordeaux-style blend for the table, red and black fruit with a leafy edge and gentle tannin; the house red of the region.
Cooler and spicier than Barossa, red cherry and white pepper with medium body; a reminder that the region's maritime air suits grapes beyond Cabernet.

exam: Place McLaren Vale in the Fleurieu zone south of Adelaide on Gulf St Vincent, and name the sea breeze as its climate.
Give Shiraz as the lead and old bush-vine Grenache as the second claim, and spell out GSM as Grenache, Shiraz, Mataro.
Know the geology as the region's boast, more than forty units, and Blewitt Springs' sand as the Grenache district.
Name the founding facts: Reynella 1838, Hardy's Tintara 1876, d'Arenberg 1912, and no phylloxera.
Recognise the Mediterranean varieties, Fiano, Vermentino, Tempranillo and Nero d'Avola, as the region's modern direction.
At Advanced, list the Fleurieu zone's other regions and know Langhorne Creek's Cabernet and Bremer River flooding.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Full-bodied with blackberry, plum and dark chocolate, a savoury, almost salty edge and softer tannin than the Barossa; the region's identity and the subject of its single-vineyard Scarce Earth bottlings.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: Old bush vines on sand, some planted in the 1940s, giving perfumed raspberry and red cherry, sandy tannin and mid-weight charm; now made with whole bunches and old wood, and the region's fastest-rising wine.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripe blackcurrant and dark chocolate, softer and warmer than Coonawarra, alone or with Shiraz and Merlot in blends such as Church Block.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: Mataro from old vines, meaty, dark and firm, the M of the GSM blend and occasionally bottled alone.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: Among the Mediterranean varieties that suit the warm dry summer, giving cherry, leather and moderate tannin.

grapes.name: Fiano
grapes.styles: A southern Italian white, textural, honeyed and herbal, that keeps its acid in heat better than Chardonnay and has become a regional signature white.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: Crisp, saline and citrus-led, a summer white for the beaches an hour from the vineyards.

grapes.name: Nero d’Avola
grapes.styles: Sicily's red, dark-fruited and spicy, planted for its ease in heat.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown mostly in the cooler hills around Clarendon and Kangarilla for a ripe, peachy white.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: Australia's first commercial planting was here in 1985; savoury, cherry-led and medium-bodied.

law.classification: McLaren Vale is a registered region of the Fleurieu zone, which also holds Langhorne Creek, Currency Creek, Southern Fleurieu and Kangaroo Island. The GI is a line on the map and no more; the 85 per cent rule for variety, vintage and origin applies. The districts a server meets on labels, Blewitt Springs, Clarendon, McLaren Flat, Seaview, Willunga and the rest, are growers' names used by the regional association, not registered subregions. Scarce Earth is a regional programme for single-site Shiraz with its own tasting panel, a private mark; sustainability certification is likewise voluntary. Several of the region's Shiraz and Grenache wines sit in Langton's private classification.
labels: Scarce Earth
A regional programme of single-vineyard Shiraz approved by a tasting panel; a private mark, not a legal tier.
GSM
Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro, named in descending order of proportion under the national rule.
Church Block
Wirra Wirra's Cabernet, Shiraz and Merlot blend, named for the church beside the vineyard; a house term.
The Dead Arm
d'Arenberg's flagship Shiraz, named for the Eutypa dieback that leaves old vines with one dead arm; a house term.
tiers: Zone: Fleurieu
The peninsula zone south of Adelaide: McLaren Vale, Langhorne Creek, Currency Creek, Southern Fleurieu and Kangaroo Island.
Region: McLaren Vale
The registered GI from the Onkaparinga River south to Sellicks; 85 per cent of a McLaren Vale wine comes from inside the line.
Districts (unofficial)
Blewitt Springs, Clarendon, Kangarilla, McLaren Flat, Seaview, Willunga, Sellicks Foothills, Aldinga and others, used by growers and on labels, none registered as a subregion.

made.viticulture: Vines run from old bush vines on sand, dry grown and hand picked, to modern trellised blocks under drip irrigation and machine harvest. The region pioneered the use of recycled water for irrigation and its growers wrote the sustainability programme that grew into the national scheme for Australian vineyards, so cover crops, reduced spraying and water accounting are regional habits rather than novelties. Heat is the main hazard: a summer spike can shrivel Shiraz and push alcohol past 15 per cent, so canopies are kept full for shade and picking has moved earlier over the last two decades. Grenache is picked for perfume rather than weight, and whole bunches are kept for the ferment. The old trunk disease Eutypa, which kills one arm of a vine and leaves the other bearing, is common on old Shiraz and gave d'Arenberg's flagship its name, The Dead Arm. Phylloxera has never arrived, so vines are on their own roots. Site matters more each year: Blewitt Springs for Grenache on sand, Clarendon for cooler, later Shiraz and Chardonnay in the hills, Willunga and Seaview for the fuller, warmer styles.
made.winemaking: Shiraz is made in open fermenters with pump-overs or foot treading at the traditional houses, pressed in basket presses at d'Arenberg and a few others, and matured in French oak hogsheads and puncheons for twelve to twenty months; the American oak of the past has mostly gone. The best makers hold alcohol near 14 to 14.5 per cent by picking on flavour and blending across sites. The Scarce Earth programme bottles single-vineyard Shiraz from named sites, tasted and approved by a regional panel, so the geology can be compared glass by glass. Grenache has been remade: whole-bunch and whole-berry ferments, gentle extraction, ageing in old barrels, concrete or large vats, and no new oak, to keep the raspberry perfume and sandy tannin. GSM blends are assembled from separate parcels. The Mediterranean whites, Fiano and Vermentino, are fermented cool in stainless steel, sometimes with skin contact or lees for texture, and bottled dry under screwcap. A handful of houses make traditional-method sparkling Shiraz, dark, sweet-edged and a Christmas tradition.

places.name: Blewitt Springs
places.note: The elevated northern district on deep sand over clay, cooler than the floor and the heartland of old bush-vine Grenache, with some vines from the 1940s; fine, perfumed Shiraz too.

places.name: Clarendon
places.note: The hill district in the north-east above 300 metres, the coolest part of the region, giving later-picked Shiraz with more pepper and acid, and the region's best Chardonnay.

places.name: McLaren Flat
places.note: The alluvial centre east of the township, generous Shiraz and Grenache on loam and sand.

places.name: Seaview
places.note: The ridge west of the township towards the gulf, with ironstone and limestone, named for the old Seaview winery that stood there; ripe, saline Shiraz.

places.name: Willunga
places.note: The southern town beneath the escarpment, warm red-brown earths over limestone and the site of the regional farmers' market; full-bodied Shiraz and Cabernet.

places.name: Reynella
places.note: The northern gateway near the Onkaparinga where the first vines went in in 1838 and where the Hardy company kept its historic home.

places.name: The Fleurieu zone beyond McLaren Vale
places.note: The zone's four other regions lie east and south; a server meets Langhorne Creek on lists most often.

places.name: Langhorne Creek
places.note: East of the Mount Lofty Ranges near Lake Alexandrina, a flat region once irrigated by the winter flooding of the Bremer River, cooled by lake breezes, known for soft, generous Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz that fed many blends.

places.name: Currency Creek
places.note: Between Langhorne Creek and the Southern Ocean near Goolwa, maritime and modest, with Cabernet and Shiraz.

places.name: Southern Fleurieu
places.note: The cool, windy southern tip of the peninsula on Encounter Bay, with Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Kangaroo Island
places.note: The island off the peninsula's tip, maritime and small in vineyard, with Bordeaux varieties and Shiraz.

producers.name: d'Arenberg
producers.why: Founded in 1912 and still foot treading and basket pressing; The Dead Arm Shiraz, a long list of oddly named wines and a cube-shaped cellar door made it the region's best-known name.

producers.name: Hardys Tintara
producers.why: Thomas Hardy bought the Tintara winery in 1876, and the company he founded in 1853 became one of Australia's largest; Tintara remains its McLaren Vale home.

producers.name: Wirra Wirra
producers.why: Founded in 1894 and revived in 1969; Church Block, a Cabernet Shiraz Merlot blend, is one of Australia's best-loved everyday reds, and RSW Shiraz its flagship.

producers.name: Kay Brothers Amery
producers.why: A family winery of 1890 whose Block 6 Shiraz comes from vines planted in 1892, among the oldest in the region.

producers.name: Coriole
producers.why: Planted Australia's first commercial Sangiovese in 1985 and leads the region's Italian turn with Fiano and Nero d'Avola beside its old-vine Shiraz.

producers.name: Yangarra Estate
producers.why: A biodynamic estate at Blewitt Springs whose High Sands Grenache, from bush vines planted in 1946, is the reference for the modern style.

producers.name: Chapel Hill
producers.why: A house named for its 1865 stone chapel, known for balanced Shiraz, Grenache and Mediterranean whites.

terroir.climate: Warm Mediterranean with a maritime brake: hot dry summers, mild wet winters with 550 to 650 millimetres of rain, and an afternoon sea breeze off Gulf St Vincent that drops the temperature and keeps acid in the fruit. Frost is almost unknown and rot pressure is low. Sites climb from sea level to over 300 metres at Clarendon, so harvest dates spread across March and April and a cool hill block and a warm sandy one can be weeks apart.
terroir.soils: The region's boast and its geologists' delight: more than forty distinct geological units mapped across a small area, from ancient rock to recent sand. Blewitt Springs has deep, pale sands over clay that suit Grenache bush vines; McLaren Flat and the central floor sit on alluvial loams; Willunga and the Sellicks foothills on red-brown earths over limestone and ironstone; Clarendon on older, rockier hill soils. The variety is the argument behind the region's single-site Shiraz.
terroir.topography: A broad amphitheatre opening west to the gulf, the Willunga escarpment and the Sellicks Hill Range forming its eastern and southern wall, the Onkaparinga River gorge its northern edge, and the land stepping down from Clarendon and Kangarilla in the hills through Blewitt Springs and McLaren Flat to Willunga, Aldinga and the coast.
terroir.water: Gulf St Vincent gives the afternoon breeze and the saline note tasters find in the Shiraz; the Onkaparinga River bounds the north. Irrigation leans on treated, recycled water piped from Adelaide through a regional scheme, a practical answer to a dry summer that the region has used since the end of the 1990s.

traps: McLaren Vale is in the Fleurieu zone, not the Mount Lofty Ranges zone, though the ranges form its eastern wall.
Mataro is Mourvèdre; GSM is Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro in descending order, not a fixed recipe.
The districts, Blewitt Springs and the rest, are unofficial; the region has no registered subregion.
McLaren Vale Shiraz is savoury and chocolatey with a saline edge, softer than Barossa, warmer than Coonawarra; do not call it jammy by default.
The Dead Arm is a Shiraz named for a vine disease, Eutypa dieback, not for a style or a vineyard.
Scarce Earth is a regional single-vineyard programme with a tasting panel, not a classification in law.

wines.note: Full-bodied and generous, blackberry, plum, dark chocolate and liquorice with a savoury, faintly salty finish and soft, round tannin; mostly French oak now. Serve just below room temperature with braised beef, barbecued lamb or a mushroom ragù.

From old bush vines on sand: raspberry, red cherry, rose and dried herbs, mid-weight with fine sandy tannin and little new oak, like a sunny Châteauneuf without the weight. Serve slightly cool with roast pork, duck or charcuterie.
Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro, the southern Rhône model: spice, red and black fruit, earth and warmth, friendly young and good with lamb, sausages and grilled vegetables.
Ripe blackcurrant and chocolate with a eucalypt lift and soft tannin, rounder than Coonawarra's; often blended with Shiraz and Merlot.
Textural and dry, pear, honeysuckle and almond with firm acid, the region's modern white for seafood, grilled fish and salty antipasti.

exam: Name the grape of Rutherglen Muscat, Brown Muscat, and give its formal name, Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge.
Name the grape of Topaque, Muscadelle, and the name it replaced, Tokay, lost under the 2008 EU agreement.
Recite the ladder in order: Rutherglen, Classic, Grand, Rare, and say that it is the producers' classification of 1995, not law.
Explain the method in a sentence: raisined on the vine, briefly fermented, fortified with spirit, aged oxidatively for years in old wood in hot sheds, blended across ages.
Place it: north-east Victoria on the Murray, hot continental; name Glenrowan as the sister fortified region.
Know Durif as the dry red and its alias Petite Sirah.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Brown Muscat, the red-skinned Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge, raisined on the vine and fortified: the grape of Rutherglen Muscat, all raisin, rose, toffee and rancio.

grapes.name: Muscadelle
grapes.styles: The grape of Topaque, once labelled Tokay; the same raisining and fortifying gives cold tea, malt, toffee and honey rather than Muscat's grapey perfume.

grapes.name: Durif
grapes.styles: The region's dry red signature since its introduction in the early twentieth century: deep, dense, tannic and plummy, the same grape as California's Petite Sirah.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Full-bodied, ripe and generous, often with a dried-fruit edge; also a base of the region's vintage fortified wines.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Planted for the vintage fortified wines that once wore the Port name; blended with Shiraz and Durif.

law.classification: Rutherglen is a registered region of the North East Victoria zone, with Beechworth, Glenrowan, King Valley and Alpine Valleys as its neighbours in the zone; it has no subregions. The GI fixes the boundary and nothing else, and the ordinary 85 per cent rules apply to region, variety and vintage. The Muscat ladder is not law: the Muscat of Rutherglen Network, a producers' association, created the four-tier classification in 1995 and polices it among its members, with Rutherglen, Classic, Grand and Rare rising in richness, complexity and average age. Under the 2008 agreement on trade in wine between Australia and the European Community the region gave up the borrowed names Tokay and Port; Tokay became Topaque and the Port-style wines became vintage fortified.
labels: Topaque
Fortified Muscadelle, the wine formerly labelled Tokay; the name is the Rutherglen producers' own.
Brown Muscat
The local name for Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge, the red-skinned clone behind Rutherglen Muscat.
Rancio
The nutty, oxidative character of long wood age, prized in Grand and Rare wines.
Vintage fortified
The Port style made from Shiraz, Durif and Touriga, labelled without the Portuguese name since the EU agreement.
Durif
The region's signature dry red grape, identical to Petite Sirah.
tiers: Zone: North East Victoria
Rutherglen, Glenrowan, Beechworth, King Valley and Alpine Valleys; a blend across them claims the zone.
Region: Rutherglen
The registered GI and the label claim; 85 per cent of the fruit from inside the boundary.
Rutherglen Muscat (the first rung)
The network's base tier: fresh, raisiny and grapey, the youngest blends, indicatively three to five years' average age.
Classic Rutherglen Muscat
More depth and some rancio; indicatively six to ten years' average age.
Grand Rutherglen Muscat
Rich, dark and complex, with marked rancio; indicatively eleven to nineteen years' average age.
Rare Rutherglen Muscat
The pinnacle, a blend built on the oldest reserves, indicatively twenty years and more of average age, released in small quantities.

made.viticulture: The Muscat and Muscadelle vines are grown to hang: moderate crops, low trellised or bush vines in open rows, and a harvest that waits deep into autumn while the berries shrivel on the vine and the sugar climbs past the level any table wine would want, often above 20 degrees Baumé. The dry, warm autumn makes this possible without the rot that would ruin it in a humid region. Picking is by hand in passes, selecting the most raisined bunches, and the dry-red grapes come in earlier at ordinary ripeness. Phylloxera devastated the district in the 1890s, so the vines are grafted and the region sits inside a declared phylloxera infested zone; the ancient own-rooted vines the Barossa boasts are not found here. Durif was introduced in the early twentieth century through the government viticulturist François de Castella and thrived in the heat. Irrigation from the Murray supports the dry wines; the old Muscat blocks are often dry grown. Frost, heat and birds are the ordinary enemies.
made.winemaking: The raisined grapes are crushed and a short fermentation begins, often only a day or two, before neutral grape spirit is added to stop it, leaving most of the sugar and lifting the wine to around 17 to 18 per cent alcohol. The young fortified wine then goes to old oak casks of every size, in iron-roofed sheds without climate control, where heat and slow oxidation concentrate and darken it over years and decades. Each house holds reserves of great age and blends across them, a modified solera that is not a strict Jerez system, so a bottle is a blend of many years and the ladder term describes the blend's average age and richness rather than a vintage. Fresh young material is added to keep the perfume; the oldest material, sometimes a century in wood, is used by the spoonful. Topaque is made the same way from Muscadelle. Durif and Shiraz are made as big dry reds with warm fermentations and oak, and the vintage fortifieds are stopped with spirit young and bottled to age.

places.name: Rutherglen township and the loams
places.note: The town and the gentle rises around it on red Rutherglen loam hold the oldest houses, Chambers Rosewood (1858), Morris (1859), Campbells (1870) and Stanton & Killeen (1875), with their cask sheds full of reserves a century old.

places.name: Wahgunyah
places.note: The river town north-west of Rutherglen, right on the Murray opposite Corowa, where All Saints Estate, founded in 1864, stands with its castle-like winery among the river gums on sandier alluvial soils near the water.

places.name: Glenrowan (neighbour)
places.note: A separate region of the same zone to the south-west, Ned Kelly country, with its own fortified Muscat and Topaque tradition at Baileys of Glenrowan (1870); the exam pairs the two.

places.name: Beechworth (neighbour)
places.note: A cool, higher granite region of the zone in the hills to the south-east, better known for Chardonnay and Shiraz than for fortifieds; a different world an hour away.

places.name: King Valley and Alpine Valleys (neighbours)
places.note: The zone's other regions, running up the King and Ovens rivers into the Alps, cooler with elevation and home to Italian varieties and sparkling; not fortified country.

producers.name: Chambers Rosewood
producers.why: Founded 1858; its Rare Muscat and Rare Topaque are blends built on reserves older than anyone alive, and the benchmark of the top rung.

producers.name: Morris of Rutherglen
producers.why: Founded 1859; Old Premium Rare Muscat and Topaque of great density, from one of the deepest reserve cellars in the district.

producers.name: Campbells
producers.why: Founded 1870; its Rare Muscat and Rare Topaque carry proprietary names, and its Bobbie Burns Shiraz is the dry-red calling card.

producers.name: All Saints Estate
producers.why: Founded 1864 at Wahgunyah by the river, with a winery built like a Scottish castle; Rare Muscat and Topaque and the region's showpiece cellar door.

producers.name: Stanton & Killeen
producers.why: Founded 1875; the house most devoted to the vintage fortified style, alongside Muscat, Topaque and Durif.

producers.name: Buller Wines
producers.why: Founded 1921; Rare Muscat and Topaque under the Calliope name, and sturdy Durif.

terroir.climate: Hot continental, with scorching dry summers, cool nights and a long warm autumn that lets fruit hang and shrivel into raisins on the vine without rot. Rain falls mainly in winter and spring; the growing season is dry, so irrigation is normal for the dry wines. Frost is a spring hazard on the flat ground and heat spikes a summer one.
terroir.soils: Deep red loams and sandy loams over clay on gentle rises, the so-called Rutherglen loam, with sandier alluvial ground towards the river. They hold water well enough for old dry-grown vines, drain adequately, and make the dark, full-bodied Durif and Shiraz the region is known for alongside the fortifieds.
terroir.topography: Flat to gently rolling plains at around 150 to 200 metres, with the Murray floodplain to the north and the foothills of the Victorian Alps rising to the south-east towards Beechworth; the town stands on a low rise between the river and the hills. There is no shelter from the sun and little from the wind.
terroir.water: The Murray River, Australia's great river, runs along the region's northern edge and the state border, with Lake Mulwala downstream and the Hume reservoir upstream; it supplies irrigation but does little to cool the air. Lake Moodemere, a billabong beside the town, is the local landmark.

traps: Topaque was Tokay but has nothing to do with Hungary's Tokaji: the grape is Muscadelle of Bordeaux, not Furmint.
Muscat here is Brown Muscat, the red-skinned Petits Grains clone, not the white Muscat of Alsace nor the Muscat of Alexandria behind Spain's Moscatel.
The Rutherglen ladder is a trademark of a producers' network, not a government tier; the GI itself grades nothing.

Rutherglen Muscat is fortified and oxidatively aged, so it is not a late-harvest wine and not a botrytis wine; the fortification idea is shared with the vins doux naturels of the French south, the raisining and the hot-shed ageing are not.
Rutherglen is not Riverina: the botrytis Semillon stickies come from Griffith in New South Wales, not from north-east Victoria.
A Rare Muscat carries no vintage; it is a blend of many years, and its age is indicative of the blend, never a single harvest.

wines.note: Dark amber to walnut, sweet and viscous, tasting of raisin, rose, toffee and burnt orange, with the nutty rancio of long oxidative ageing, at around 17 to 18 per cent. Serve it cool in a small glass after dinner, with blue cheese, sticky toffee pudding or chocolate, or alone.
The Muscadelle sibling: cold tea, malt, butterscotch, honey and dried fig, a touch less perfumed and a touch more savoury than the Muscat. Same service, same ladder, same sheds.
Inky, full-bodied, tannic and plummy, with chocolate and spice; a steak or braise wine that needs air and years.
Shiraz, Durif and Touriga fortified young and bottled to age, sweet and tannic; made under the Port name until the EU agreement retired it.

exam: Say what Tasmania is in law: one GI for the whole state, a zone and region in one, with no registered subregions.
Name the grapes in order: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Riesling, and say sparkling is the island's calling card.
Place the districts: Tamar Valley and Pipers River in the north, East Coast, Coal River, Derwent and Huon in the south-east; the west grows nothing.
Explain the rain shadow: westerlies soak the west, the east is dry and irrigated.
Know Jansz (Pipers River, 1986 Roederer joint venture) and House of Arras (1995) as the sparkling names, and that mainland houses buy Tasmanian base wine.
Phylloxera free, like South Australia; climate cool maritime, latitude 41 to 43 south.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The most planted grape and the island's red: bright, fine and fragrant from the Coal River and the Tamar, and the backbone of the sparkling blends.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Lean, citrus-driven and long-lived, from the Tamar, Pipers River and the East Coast, and the other half of the sparkling base.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Crisp and herbal, a cool-climate style between Marlborough and the Loire, mostly from the north and east.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Textural, pear-scented dry whites, often in the Alsace manner, a growing share of the island's whites.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Dry and fine, with lime and florals, from the Coal River and Derwent valleys; some off-dry and late-harvest styles.

grapes.name: Pinot Meunier
grapes.styles: The third sparkling grape, grown in small amounts for the traditional-method blends.

law.classification: Tasmania is one registered Geographical Indication covering the whole state: it serves as its own zone and its own region, and no subregion has been registered, so Tamar Valley, Pipers River, Coal River Valley, Derwent Valley, Huon Valley, East Coast and North West are trade descriptions with no legal boundary; the legal claim on the label is Tasmania. The 85 per cent rule applies to that claim, to the variety and to the vintage, and blends list their grapes largest first. A mainland house that buys Tasmanian fruit may label the wine Tasmania if 85 per cent of it is Tasmanian, which is how the island's name appears on bottles finished far away. The state's phylloxera quarantine is agricultural law, not wine labelling law.
labels: Tasmania
The origin claim: 85 per cent of the fruit from the island.
Late disgorged (LD)
A sparkling wine given extra years on lees before disgorgement; a house term.
Blanc de Blancs
Sparkling wine from white grapes only, here Chardonnay.
Vintage sparkling
A single year named on the label; 85 per cent of the wine from that year.
Brut
Dry sparkling wine; the term follows the Champagne scale by convention rather than Australian law.
tiers: GI: Tasmania
The whole state, a zone and a region in one; the only legal origin claim an island wine carries.
District names (unregistered)
Tamar Valley, Pipers River, Coal River Valley, Derwent Valley, Huon Valley, East Coast, North West: descriptions, not GIs.
South Eastern Australia
The super-zone that includes Tasmania entire, used for multi-state blends.

made.viticulture: Ripening is the whole game. Sites are chosen on sunny slopes in the rain shadow, rows run to catch the light, canopies are opened by leaf plucking, crops are kept moderate, and harvest comes late, from March into May, with sparkling bases picked first at high acid and modest sugar and the Pinot and Chardonnay for table wine following. Wind is a constant and shelter belts are planted; frost is fought with fans and water; netting against birds is universal because the island has few other crops to tempt them. The east needs irrigation from dams; the wetter north around Pipers River needs spraying against botrytis and mildew instead. The island is phylloxera free and guards its borders with quarantine, so the vines are own-rooted or grafted as the grower chooses. Clonal selection of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay is a preoccupation, and the state's small vineyards are tended at a density and detail closer to Burgundy than to the Riverland. Mainland companies run large vineyards here for sparkling base and ship the fruit or the base wine north.
made.winemaking: Sparkling wine is the traditional method with the full apparatus: whole-bunch pressing, a cool primary fermentation, partial malolactic conversion as the maker chooses, reserve wines in some houses, a second fermentation in bottle and lees ageing from eighteen months for the entry cuvées to many years for the prestige and late-disgorged bottlings that carry the island's name. Pinot Noir is made in open fermenters with a share of whole bunches and aged in French barriques with a restrained share of new wood. Chardonnay is barrel-fermented on solids and kept lean, with the malolactic conversion often stopped to hold the acid. Rieslings are fermented cool in steel, some left with a little sugar; Pinot Gris may see lees or old oak for texture. The characteristic choice everywhere is restraint, because the fruit has acid and perfume to spare and needs no help from the cellar.

places.name: Tamar Valley
places.note: The estuary north of Launceston, the island's historic centre of volume, with vineyards on both banks; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Gris and sparkling. Mild, sunny for Tasmania and sheltered.

places.name: Pipers River
places.note: North-east of the Tamar towards the Bass Strait coast, wetter and cooler, on red basalt soils: the island's sparkling heartland since the 1970s and 1980s, where Pipers Brook, Jansz, Clover Hill and Bay of Fires grew. Also fine Pinot and Chardonnay.

places.name: East Coast
places.note: Bicheno, Swansea and the Freycinet coast, dry, sunny and sea-moderated: generous Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with Freycinet Vineyard the pioneer from 1980.

places.name: Coal River Valley
places.note: North-east of Hobart around Richmond and Cambridge, dry, warm by island standards and frost-prone on the flats, on dolerite clays and sandstone: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Riesling of great definition, and the Tolpuddle and Domaine A vineyards. Irrigated from stored water.

places.name: Derwent Valley
places.note: Up the Derwent north-west of Hobart, sheltered river slopes with Moorilla at Berriedale, planted in 1958, one of the first vineyards of the island's modern era and still working; Pinot, Chardonnay, Riesling and sparkling.

places.name: Huon Valley and the Channel
places.note: South of Hobart, Australia's southernmost vineyards, cool and marginal, apple country turned to Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling; small estates.

places.name: North West
places.note: Around Devonport and the Mersey, on red basalt soils in a cool, wet maritime setting; a small district with sparkling and Pinot ambitions.

producers.name: Jansz Tasmania
producers.why: Born of a 1986 joint venture between Heemskerk and Louis Roederer at Pipers River, an early Tasmanian house built for traditional-method sparkling alone and the island's best known label abroad.

producers.name: House of Arras
producers.why: Founded 1995; long-lees-aged vintage sparkling wines, Grand Vintage, Blanc de Blancs and late-disgorged cuvées, that set the island's prestige standard.

producers.name: Pipers Brook Vineyard
producers.why: Planted 1974 at Pipers River; the estate that argued, on paper and in the glass, that the cool north could ripen Pinot, Chardonnay and Riesling.

producers.name: Freycinet Vineyard
producers.why: The East Coast's pioneer at Bicheno from 1980; Pinot Noir from a sunny amphitheatre, and sparkling.

producers.name: Moorilla
producers.why: Planted 1958 at Berriedale on the Derwent by Claudio Alcorso, one of the island's first modern vineyards, two years after Providence in the Tamar; Pinot, Chardonnay, Riesling and sparkling.

producers.name: Tolpuddle Vineyard
producers.why: A single Coal River Valley site planted in 1988 whose Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are among the island's most sought.

producers.name: Domaine A
producers.why: A Coal River estate on the Stoney Vineyard, known for the island's most serious Cabernet Sauvignon, proof that the warm, dry valley can ripen it.

producers.name: Clover Hill
producers.why: A Pipers River estate planted in 1986 for traditional-method sparkling wine alone.

terroir.climate: Cool maritime, the coolest mainstream wine climate in Australia, with a long, slow ripening season, high natural acidity and a real risk of not ripening fully in a poor year. The west is drenched by the prevailing westerlies and grows no vines; the east sits in the rain shadow of the central highlands and is dry enough to need irrigation. Spring frost, wind, botrytis in the wetter north and birds are the hazards.
terroir.soils: Varied by district. Jurassic dolerite, the dark rock that caps the island's mountains, weathers to the clays of the Coal River and Derwent valleys; Tertiary basalt gives the deep red ferrosols of Pipers River and the North West; the Tamar's soils are mixed; sandstone and river alluvium appear in the east and south. Free-draining sites on slopes are chosen to shed the cold air and the water.
terroir.topography: A mountainous island with the Central Plateau at its heart; the vineyards keep to low hills and valley sides below about 300 metres, on north and east-facing slopes that catch the sun and drain the frost. The north faces Bass Strait across the Tamar estuary and the Pipers River coast; the east faces the Tasman Sea; the south-east around Hobart is a maze of estuaries and sheltered valleys.
terroir.water: The sea is never far and sets the climate: Bass Strait to the north, the Tasman Sea to the east, the Southern Ocean beyond. The Tamar estuary and the Derwent and Huon rivers give their valleys their names and their mildness; the Coal River is a small stream in a dry valley that farms on stored water.

traps: Tamar Valley on a label is a description, not a GI; the registered claim is Tasmania, and any subregion claim would need registering first.
Tasmania is cool but not uniformly wet: the Coal River and East Coast are dry enough to irrigate, so do not call every Tasmanian vineyard cold and damp.
Tasmanian Pinot is lighter and finer than Central Otago's; Central Otago is continental, Tasmania maritime.
A sparkling wine labelled Tasmania may be finished on the mainland; the claim is about the fruit, not the cellar.
Jansz began as a Heemskerk and Louis Roederer joint venture in 1986; the name honours Abel Janszoon Tasman, the Dutch navigator, so say it the Dutch way.
The island's southernmost vineyards, in the Huon, are Australia's southernmost, but its warmest district is not in the north: the Coal River near Hobart is among the warmest and driest.

wines.note: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, sometimes Meunier, bottle-fermented and aged on lees for years in the top cuvées; taut, fine-beaded, citrus and brioche, with the acidity of a cold climate. Serve it as you would Champagne.
Cherry, cranberry and spice, fresh acid and fine tannin, lighter than Central Otago and often compared with the Yarra; a food wine for duck, salmon and mushrooms, served slightly cool.
Citrus, green apple and oyster shell, flinty, long and lean, with oak in the background; it ages well. Pour it with the island's oysters, crayfish and trout.
Dry, lime and blossom, high acid, sometimes with a little residual sugar to balance; a cold-climate white for oysters and Asian dishes.
Crisp aromatic whites from the north and east, Sauvignon herbal and citrus, Pinot Gris pear and spice with weight; the island's everyday glasses.
wines.style: Tasmanian Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris

exam: Place the Yarra: Victoria, north-east of Melbourne, in the Port Phillip zone with Mornington Peninsula, Geelong, Macedon Ranges and Sunbury.
Name the grapes in order of fame: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, sparkling, then Cabernet blends and cool Shiraz.
Know the history dates: planted 1838 at Yering, dormant from 1921, revived from the 1960s (Yarra Yering 1969, Mount Mary 1971), Domaine Chandon 1986.
Upper against Lower Yarra: higher, cooler, red volcanic soils against lower, warmer, grey sedimentary loams.
Climate class: cool, often set beside Burgundy; frost, autumn rain and smoke are the hazards.
The houses: Mount Mary (Quintet), Yarra Yering (Dry Red No. 1 and No. 2), Yeringberg, Coldstream Hills, Domaine Chandon.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The flagship red: perfumed, red-fruited and fine-boned, from light and silky on the valley floor to deeper and darker in the Upper Yarra; among the most Burgundian Pinots on the mainland.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Taut, citrus and white peach with struck-match and oatmeal notes from barrel; the region helped lead Australia's turn from fat, buttery Chardonnay to the lean modern style.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The historic grape of the valley's 1860s heyday and of its revival estates: cassis, leaf and cedar in Bordeaux-style blends with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petit Verdot, medium-bodied and long-lived.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Cool-climate Shiraz, often labelled Syrah: pepper, red fruit and spice, sometimes with a splash of Viognier, closer to the northern Rhône than to the Barossa.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: A partner in the Cabernet blends of the old estates and occasionally a varietal; soft, plummy and leafy here.

law.classification: The Yarra Valley is a registered region in the Port Phillip zone, the zone that also holds Mornington Peninsula, Geelong, Macedon Ranges and Sunbury; it has no registered subregions, so Upper Yarra and Lower Yarra are descriptions, not claims. As everywhere in Australia, the GI fixes the border and nothing more; grape, yield, density and ageing are the producer's choice. The 85 per cent rule applies to region, variety and vintage, and blends are named in descending order, so a Shiraz Viognier has more Shiraz than Viognier. A wine blending Yarra and Mornington fruit may claim Port Phillip or Victoria. Phylloxera infested zones are an agricultural matter, not a labelling one.
labels: Shiraz Viognier
A co-fermented blend; the grape named first is the larger share.
Syrah
Some cool-climate makers use the French name to signal a peppery, medium-bodied style; it is the same grape as Shiraz.
Dry Red No. 1 and No. 2
Yarra Yering's house names: No. 1 is the Cabernet blend, No. 2 the Shiraz blend.
Quintet
Mount Mary's Cabernet blend of five Bordeaux grapes; a house name, not a term of law.
Single vineyard
Unregulated; it means what the producer says it means.
tiers: Zone: Port Phillip
The zone around Melbourne: Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula, Geelong, Macedon Ranges and Sunbury; a label claiming Port Phillip may blend across them.
Region: Yarra Valley
The registered unit and the usual claim; 85 per cent of the fruit from inside the line.
Upper Yarra and Lower Yarra
Trade descriptions with no legal standing: higher, cooler, red soils above; lower, warmer, grey soils below.
State: Victoria
The state-wide claim that multi-region blends use; wider still are South Eastern Australia and Australia.

made.viticulture: Planting density rose with the revival: the estates of the 1970s used wide rows for the tractor, the newer plantings go closer and lower in the Burgundian manner. Vertical shoot positioning is standard, leaf plucking opens the fruit zone to light in a climate where ripeness is earned, and crop levels are kept down for Pinot. Harvest runs from late February for sparkling bases through March for Chardonnay and Pinot into April for Cabernet, with the Upper Yarra a fortnight or more behind the floor. The hazards are frost in the low pockets, botrytis after autumn rain, birds, and smoke taint from bushfire. Phylloxera was found in the valley in 2006, ending its own-rooted innocence; growers now replant on resistant rootstock and the state runs quarantine zones. Water comes from dams and the river; irrigation is a supplement, not a system, on the water-holding red soils. Clone choice matters: the old Pinot clone MV6 and the Dijon clones each have their partisans.
made.winemaking: Pinot Noir is made along Burgundian lines: a cold soak, open fermenters, a proportion of whole bunches that the maker argues over, gentle plunging, a year or so in French barriques with a modest share new, and bottling with little fining. Chardonnay is pressed whole bunch, fermented in barrel on its solids with wild yeast at many houses, and kept on lees with the malolactic conversion partly or wholly blocked to hold the line; the fat, buttery style of the 1990s has gone. Sparkling wine is traditional method with long lees ageing for the top cuvées. Cabernet blends are fermented warm and aged in French oak for up to two years, in the restrained, claret-like idiom the estates have kept since the 1970s. Shiraz may be co-fermented with Viognier in the Côte-Rôtie fashion and sees older oak.

places.name: Lower Yarra
places.note: The valley floor and northern slopes around Yarra Glen, Coldstream, Dixons Creek, Healesville and Lilydale, lower and warmer, on the old grey loams: the historic estates and the Cabernet and Shiraz sites are mostly here, with Pinot and Chardonnay beside them. A description, not a GI.

places.name: Gruyere and Coldstream
places.note: Gruyere is Yarra Yering's address since 1969; Coldstream holds Coldstream Hills (1985) and Domaine Chandon's Green Point winery (1986). North-facing slopes that ripen Cabernet and Shiraz as well as Pinot.

places.name: Lilydale
places.note: The old town at the valley's mouth and Mount Mary's address since 1971; the Quintet Cabernet blend and the house's Pinot and Chardonnay come from here.

places.name: Yarra Glen and Yering
places.note: The cradle of Victorian wine: Yering was planted in 1838, and St Huberts and Yeringberg followed in the 1860s. Yeringberg, replanted in 1969 on its original site, links the two eras.

places.name: Dixons Creek and Healesville
places.note: The northern and eastern fringes against the ranges; Healesville's higher ground is cooler and suits Pinot and Chardonnay, and several single-vineyard specialists cellar there.

places.name: Upper Yarra
places.note: The higher southern and eastern reaches, Seville, Hoddles Creek, Gladysdale, Wandin and Yarra Junction, up to 400 metres on red volcanic soils: cooler, wetter, later, and the source of much of the finest Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling base. A description, not a GI.

places.name: Hoddles Creek
places.note: The coldest well-known pocket, where Pinot and Chardonnay ripen late with a nervy acid line; sparkling houses and the top Pinot specialists draw fruit here.

places.name: Seville
places.note: Red soils and the valley's early revival estate, Seville Estate (1972); fine Pinot, Chardonnay and a notable cool-climate Shiraz.

producers.name: Mount Mary
producers.why: Founded 1971 at Lilydale; its Quintet Cabernet blend and its Pinot Noir are the valley's most quietly prized wines, made in a restrained style that has never chased fashion.

producers.name: Yarra Yering
producers.why: Founded 1969 at Gruyere by Dr Bailey Carrodus; its Dry Red No. 1 (Cabernet) and No. 2 (Shiraz) set the revival's standard.

producers.name: Yeringberg
producers.why: Planted in 1863 by Baron Guillaume de Pury and replanted in 1969 by his descendants on the original site; Marsanne Roussanne and Cabernet blends of old-fashioned finesse.

producers.name: Coldstream Hills
producers.why: Founded 1985 at Coldstream; a Pinot Noir and Chardonnay specialist whose reserve wines helped define the valley's modern style.

producers.name: Domaine Chandon
producers.why: Moët & Chandon's Australian arm from 1986 at Green Point, Coldstream; traditional-method sparkling wine and the valley's most visited cellar door.

producers.name: De Bortoli Yarra Valley
producers.why: The Riverina family's Yarra estate from 1987 at Dixons Creek; Pinot, Chardonnay and Shiraz Viognier at every price, and an early mover in the lean modern style.

producers.name: Giant Steps
producers.why: A Healesville house built on single-vineyard Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from Upper and Lower Yarra sites, bottled separately to show the difference.

producers.name: Oakridge
producers.why: At Coldstream; its 864 series of single-site Chardonnays and Pinots are among the most sought wines in the valley.

producers.name: Yering Station
producers.why: On the site of the 1838 planting at Yering; Pinot, Chardonnay, Shiraz Viognier and sparkling, the valley's historical anchor.

producers.name: TarraWarra Estate
producers.why: Founded 1983 near Yarra Glen; estate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from a single large site.

terroir.climate: Cool for Australia, with a heat summation often set beside Burgundy or a cooler Bordeaux year, though sunnier than either. The valley floor is warmer and drier; the Upper Yarra, higher and nearer the ranges, is cooler and wetter and ripens later. Spring frost in the low pockets, autumn rain at harvest and bushfire smoke in a bad year are the hazards. There is enough warmth and sunshine for Cabernet on favoured sites, which few true cool regions can say.
terroir.soils: Two families. The older sedimentary soils of the valley floor and the north, grey-brown sandy clay loams over clay, are of low fertility and give fine, firm wines, Cabernet and Pinot among them. The younger red volcanic soils of the Upper Yarra around Seville, Hoddles Creek and Gladysdale, weathered from basalt, are deep, fertile and water-holding, and make vigorous vines and generous Chardonnay and Pinot.
terroir.topography: A broad valley opening south-west towards Melbourne, with the Great Dividing Range to the north and the Dandenong Ranges to the south. Vineyards run from below 100 metres on the floor at Yarra Glen and Coldstream to around 400 metres in the Upper Yarra foothills. Aspect and height matter more than distance: a north-facing slope at Coldstream ripens Cabernet, while a cool fold at Hoddles Creek is Pinot country.
terroir.water: The Yarra River, Melbourne's river, winds through the valley from the ranges, with its tributaries and the reservoirs that supply the city. The river moderates little; the climate comes from height and latitude, with Port Phillip Bay and Bass Strait well to the south.

traps: Yarra Valley is not Barossa: a Yarra Shiraz is peppery and medium-bodied, and a Yarra Cabernet is claret-like, not jammy.
Upper Yarra and Lower Yarra are trade descriptions; the GI is Yarra Valley alone and the zone is Port Phillip, not Yarra.
Mount Mary's Quintet is a Cabernet blend, not a Pinot; Yarra Yering's Dry Red No. 1 is Cabernet, No. 2 is Shiraz.
Domaine Chandon's cellar is in the Yarra, but its sparkling wines may draw on several Victorian regions; read the label's claim.
Victoria's oldest region is the Yarra (1838), not Rutherglen (vines from the 1850s); but the Yarra was out of wine for forty years and Rutherglen never stopped.
